node.label: Eleanor Flexner
node.date_label: Women’s rights, labour, and political struggle · 1959
node.description: Reconstructs women’s rights organizing alongside labor, education, abolition and Black women’s activity before the 1960s. Her account makes the boundaries of a movement a historical question: contemporary and later readers disagree about its suffrage emphasis, structural explanation and exclusions.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Century of Struggle: The Woman’s Rights Movement in the United States (1959; later revised and enlarged editions). Publication, reception, and subsequent revision belong to different moments.
node.scope_note: The 1959 publication, 1975 revision and later editions are separate moments. James praises expanded coverage but calls for a private-property explanation; Ostrander questions integration of other reforms while recognizing the book’s narrower declared purpose. Rupp values archival reach and race/class breadth but questions absent other women of color and private relationships. Her 1992 account mediates Flexner’s use of Schomburg, Howard, Terrell and Women’s Trade Union League records. Original prefatory and archival passages remain to be collated; this is neither an exhaustive history of women nor proof that later feminist history begins with a single book.

incident_edges.relationship: places women’s rights organizing alongside labor and Black women’s activity before the 1960s
incident_edges.evidence_note: James and Rupp identify broader coverage while offering different criticisms. Later women’s history is neither a uniform continuation nor a field founded by this book alone. Original 1959 text and later editions remain distinct.

incident_edges.relationship: makes women’s rights organizing an object of political history while exposing disputed movement boundaries
incident_edges.evidence_note: Ostrander questions causal integration of other reforms; Rupp distinguishes historical self-definition from broadened categories. These receptions clarify the political-history contribution without settling the disagreement.

incident_edges.relationship: Black historical collections and Terrell’s papers supply documentary resources for Flexner’s wider coverage
incident_edges.evidence_note: Rupp p. 163 identifies Schomburg, Howard and Terrell collections in Flexner’s bibliography. This is mediated evidence of documentary use, not direct personal advice, consultation of those archives here or a claim that Black women’s activity was fully covered.
incident_edges.map_label: Schomburg, Howard and Terrell documentary resources

incident_edges.relationship: Rupp questions the limits of movement categories and the absence of private relationships in Flexner’s account
incident_edges.evidence_note: Available 1992 passages value the inclusion of Black and white working women while questioning other exclusions and distinguishing historical self-identification from broader collective activity. Missing preview pages are not inferred; this is later reception.

incident_edges.relationship: Ostrander questions suffragist self-definition and the causal integration of other reforms
incident_edges.evidence_note: The complete review recognizes extensive research and Flexner’s narrower stated aim while examining abolition, temperance and evangelical support. His criticism is a specific intervention, not the position of all political historians.

incident_edges.relationship: Frances James asks for a structural explanation through private property and a program beyond reform
incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1960 review also welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage. This particular Marxist criticism does not make the book devoid of explanation, identify James with Janet Wilson James or establish a uniform Marxist response.

records.context: Treats rights organizing as political history; reviewers dispute how fully suffrage is integrated with other reforms and how movement boundaries should be defined.

sources.title: Frances James, “Century of Women’s Struggle,” International Socialist Review 21/1 (Winter 1960), pp. 27–28.
sources.citation: Frances James, “Century of Women’s Struggle,” International Socialist Review 21/1 (Winter 1960), pp. 27–28.

verification.note: Complete contemporary review read. Welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage but criticizes the absence of a private-property explanation and program beyond reform. These are James’s judgments. Quoted preface remains mediated; the review’s Sojourner Truth speech version is not treated as a verified transcript. Frances James is not conflated with Janet Wilson James.

verification.note: Complete review read in Ohio History’s digitized volume. Praises extensive research but questions suffragist self-definition, causal integration of other reforms and treatment of temperance/evangelical support. Quotes Flexner’s narrower stated aim; this does not independently verify every book claim. Volume/pages checked; a publication year is not newly assigned without explicit issue metadata. Browser text accessible despite curl 403 responses.
